import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 200

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/200](https://www.erdosproblems.com/200)
-/

open Filter Real

namespace Erdos200

/--
The length of the longest arithmetic progression of primes in $\{1,\ldots,n\}$.
-/
noncomputable def longestPrimeArithmeticProgressions (n : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  sSup {(k : ℕ) | ∃ s ⊆ Set.Icc 1 n, s.IsAPOfLength k ∧ ∀ m ∈ s, m.Prime}

/--
Does the longest arithmetic progression of primes in $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ have length $o(\log N)$?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 5 11]
theorem erdos_200 : answer(sorry) ↔
    (fun n => (longestPrimeArithmeticProgressions n : ℝ)) =o[atTop] (fun n => log n) := by
  sorry

/--
It follows from the prime number theorem that such a progression has length $\leq(1+o(1))\log N$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5 11]
theorem erdos_200.variants.upper : ∃ (o : ℕ → ℝ) (_ : o =o[atTop] (1 : ℕ → ℝ)),
    ∀ n, longestPrimeArithmeticProgressions n ≤ (1 + o n) * log n := by
  sorry

end Erdos200

reformulations.difference: Defines the longest length using a natural-number supremum rather than an explicit maximum.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The feasible lengths always contain 0, witnessed by the empty progression. Every feasible length k equals the cardinality of its progression and hence satisfies k ≤ n because the progression lies in Set.Icc 1 n. Thus this supremum is attained and is the actual maximum; the unbounded-set default for natural-number sSup cannot occur. In scratch.lean, longest_eq_iff_maximum proves that L(n)=k iff k is feasible and bounds every feasible length.

reformulations.difference: The source gives the asymptotic bound L(N) ≤ (1+o(1)) log N; Lean asks for a single vanishing error function making the inequality hold for every natural n, including 0 and 1.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: An eventual bound can be made pointwise by changing its error function at finitely many indices. At exceptional n ≥ 2, choose the error L(n)/log(n)−1, which makes the bound an equality. At n=0 and n=1, L(n)=0 and log(n)=0, so the bound holds automatically. Finite changes preserve little-o of the constant-one function. The reverse implication is immediate. The exact global-versus-eventual equivalence is proved in scratch.lean as upper_global_iff_eventual.

review.notes: Checked all three declarations. The official source still marks the main question OPEN and states the upper bound as a consequence of the prime number theorem, agreeing with both category tags. Set.IsAPOfLength requires cardinality equal to length, so repeated primes with difference zero cannot inflate the maximum. Sorry-free experiments in /workspace/review/scratch.lean establish boundedness and attainment, L(0)=L(1)=0, L(2)=1, L(3)=2, and L(7)≥3; they also prove the main little-o condition has the expected ∀ ε>0, ∃ N, ∀ n≥N quantifiers. The scratch file compiles, and axiom checks show no reliance on sorryAx. The reviewed file matches the specified commit.
